Rectified Language Flow

A rectified-flow language model that writes 1,024 tokens at a time, with no masking and no left-to-right order. Below, ReLF-Large and an autoregressive model of the same size generate side by side on measured wall-clock time.

Block 1

At every sampling step all 1,024 positions hold a predicted token, and the whole block moves together along a short trajectory from noise to text; the autoregressive model fills the same block one token at a time. Each box is one token position, the clock is measured wall-clock time, and every frame is stored model output.

one block at a time, batch size 1

From the paper

Results

On OpenWebText with 64 function evaluations, ReLF attains lower generative perplexity than autoregressive baselines at every model size tested under matched diversity, and reflow straightens the flow for few-step generation.

From the paper

Ablations

Singular logits, Hellinger–SVD embeddings and cross-entropy training each lower generative perplexity at matched entropy, and a 32-dimensional flow space gives the best quality–diversity trade-off.

From the paper

How it works

ReLF is trained with cross-entropy on positionwise token posteriors, and its velocity is the posterior-weighted mean of the token embeddings. Singular logits capture the divergent part of the posterior analytically, leaving the network a bounded residual and guaranteeing that the flow converges to a valid token embedding.

About the replay

ModelSequential steps per blockTime per blockSpeedup, batch size 1Speedup, batch size 64Gen. PPLEntropy
  • Time per block is the median wall-clock time over 8 runs to generate one 1,024-token sequence on one GPU at batch size 1, after warm-up; runs differ by less than 0.4%. AR-Large uses KV caching and a compiled decoding step, and both models run as CUDA graphs. Speedup is AR time divided by ReLF time for a batch of 1,024-token sequences.
  • The advantage is in latency. At batch size 64 the autoregressive model uses the GPU more fully, and the ratio falls as the table shows.
  • Each box is one of the 1,024 token positions of a block, in reading order; ↵ is a newline token and <eos> the end-of-text token that separates documents. A token too long for its box is set smaller.
  • The ReLF frames are stored trajectories of the checkpoint and sampler that were timed. At every sampling step the network outputs a distribution over the vocabulary for each position; a box shows the most likely token of that distribution at that step, and a box lights up when its token changes. Before the first step the state is Gaussian noise and nothing is decoded. The 64-step setting is the stochastic sampler of the paper's main results; it injects fresh noise at every step, so its prediction keeps changing until the last step. The 16- and 32-step settings use the deterministic Euler sampler, whose prediction settles step by step.
  • Gen. PPL (under GPT-2 Large, lower is better) and unigram entropy are measured over 1,024 samples of the same checkpoint and sampler. Lowering the temperature lowers both for the autoregressive model, so compare rows at similar entropy. The 16- and 32-step rows are the model before reflow, which is what the replay shows; after two rounds of reflow the paper reports Gen. PPL 19.4 at entropy 5.41 for 16 steps and 16.2 at 5.43 for 32 steps, at the same time per step.
  • The AR-Large block is a stored evaluation sample at temperature 0.98; its first token is given and the other 1,023 are generated. Samples of both models were taken in stored order, skipping those with offensive or violent content.
